newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam blasts French radio over human rights call.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam blasts French radio over human rights call.

text.p: Vietnam's Communist Party newspaper slammed Radio France Internationale (RFI) on Friday for reporting that overseas Vietnamese groups had urged people around the globe to stage demonstrations for human rights.
The party daily Nhan Dan said RFI had cited calls from expatriate Vietnamese organisations to stage a protest this Saturday.
"RFI did not list the names of those 'organisations' because if they did the Vietnamese overseas would laugh," Nhan Dan said.

"Because those organisations, which were invented or set up by extremists, do not have the stature to represent the Vietnamese overseas community, to turn their back on the nation and the reality of the reform process in this country," it added.

RFI, the French state's overseas radio broadcasting service, said it reported that unnamed rights organisations had called for demonstrations in Paris, Bonn, Washington, Sydney and Tokyo -- but not in Vietnam itself.
RFI said its three-sentence report specified the demonstrations were called to overturn verdicts against six poeple in Vietnam, including two Buddhist monks.

RFI's Vietnamese-language service has previously been criticised by the authorities in Hanoi. The Voice of America (VOA) and the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), which also broadcast in Vietnamese, have been similarly castigated.
Vietnam hit out at the United States in August over plans by the new Asia Pacific Network, known formerly as Radio Free Asia, to begin broadcasts to the region.
A commentary in the official army newspaper said APN's aim was to undermine socialism in Asia in the same way that Radio Free Europe had been used during the Cold War against Soviet-bloc countries.
Nhan Dan disputed RFI's ability to judge the situation in Vietnam.
It said overseas organisations should first look at other countries, where millions of people -- including Vietnamese migrants -- were unemployed and struggling for the basic right to live.
"If they are powerless in the face of inequality in those countries, they would do better to be polite, keep silent, desist from slander and stop telling others how to act," it said.
